Preparing panel data

Source: vignettes/preprocess-panel.Rmd
preprocess-panel.Rmd

Intensive longitudinal data record the same persons on many occasions, and the questions they address concern processes within persons, such as whether the state of a person on one occasion relates to other states of that person on the same or the following occasion. Raw scores are an imperfect basis for these questions. Each raw score combines the stable level at which a person typically stands with the deviation of the occasion from that level, so an association computed on raw scores mixes a between-person association with a within-person association. The two associations answer different questions and can differ in size and in sign (Curran and Bauer 2011; Hoffman and Stawski 2009). A raw score also holds no information about earlier occasions, while any claim about temporal precedence requires the state on one occasion to be paired with a later state of the same person. Scores that change systematically over the study period, through learning, fatigue or habituation, share that change across variables, and a shared trend produces an association between two variables whose occasion-to-occasion fluctuations are independent.

Panel preparation removes these sources of bias before modelling. The decomposition of a variable separates its between-person and within-person components, a lagged variable pairs each occasion with the preceding occasion of the same person, and detrending removes a linear change over the study period. Each transformation is computed separately for each person and in time order.

The examples use the 36 learners in srl, each observed on 156 days.

Within-person and between-person decomposition

A variable measured repeatedly varies between persons and within persons. A learner can report high efficacy on most days because high efficacy is a stable characteristic of that learner, and the same learner reports higher efficacy on some days than on others. The two sources of variation correspond to different mechanisms. The between-person association concerns stable differences, whether learners who are generally more efficacious also generally invest more effort. The within-person association concerns a process, whether a learner invests more effort on days when that learner feels more efficacious than usual. The first characterises a population of persons and the second characterises the functioning of each person, and the inference from one to the other holds only under restrictive conditions (Molenaar 2004).

A regression of raw scores estimates a weighted combination of the two slopes, with weights given by the share of the predictor’s variance at each level (Curran and Bauer 2011). When the two slopes differ, the pooled slope matches neither, and its value depends on the composition of the sample. Entering the person mean and the deviation from it as separate predictors resolves this conflation (Mundlak 1978; Hoffman and Stawski 2009). The deviation is uncorrelated with the person mean by construction. Its slope is therefore a within-person estimate that is unaffected by any stable characteristic of the person, whether measured or unmeasured, which is the property of the fixed-effects estimator.

For a variable xx observed for person ii at occasion tt, the between-person component is the person mean, the mean of that person’s observed values, x‾i=1Ti∑t=1Tixit,\bar{x}_i = \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i} x_{it}, where TiT_i is the number of occasions on which xx was observed. The within-person component is the person-mean-centred score xit−x‾ix_{it} - \bar{x}_i, the deviation of each occasion from the person mean, and the two components sum to the original score. split_levels() adds both components to the data as variables, for efficacy as efficacy_between and efficacy_within.

split_levels(srl, id = "name", vars = "efficacy", time = "day", keep_all = FALSE) |> head()
#>    name day efficacy efficacy_within efficacy_between
#> 1 Aisha   1 38.23529      -18.684012         56.91931
#> 2 Aisha   2 14.70588      -42.213424         56.91931
#> 3 Aisha   3 67.64706       10.727753         56.91931
#> 4 Aisha   4 55.88235       -1.036953         56.91931
#> 5 Aisha   5 55.88235       -1.036953         56.91931
#> 6 Aisha   6 44.11765      -12.801659         56.91931

The between-person component efficacy_between and the within-person component efficacy_within enter the same regression as predictors of effort. The slope of efficacy_within is the within-person effect, the change in effort on days when a learner’s efficacy deviates from that learner’s mean. The slope of efficacy_between is the between-person effect, the difference in mean effort between learners whose mean efficacy differs. fit_within_between() estimates the regression on the first 124 days of each learner and holds out the last 32 days to evaluate its predictions, and the person means are computed from the estimation days only. The 4,464 estimation days are nested in 36 learners, and observations of the same learner are correlated. Standard errors that treat the observations as independent understate the uncertainty, so the standard errors are clustered on the learner (Liang and Zeger 1986).

wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort", x = "efficacy", id = "name", time = "day")
coefs(wb_fit)
#>    scope          model estimator subject subgroup             term component
#> 1 pooled within_between       ols    .all     .all      (Intercept)     .none
#> 2 pooled within_between       ols    .all     .all  efficacy_within    within
#> 3 pooled within_between       ols    .all     .all efficacy_between   between
#>   variable   estimate  std_error statistic      p_value   conf_low  conf_high
#> 1    .none 25.0284934 6.64097196  3.768800 6.059592e-04 11.5466036 38.5103833
#> 2 efficacy  0.4163891 0.05518059  7.545934 7.650039e-09  0.3043665  0.5284116
#> 3 efficacy  0.6266185 0.10584994  5.919876 9.845147e-07  0.4117317  0.8415053

The within-person slope is 0.42 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.53). On days when a learner’s efficacy is 10 points above that learner’s mean, effort is about 4 points higher. The between-person slope is 0.63 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.84). Learners whose mean efficacy is 10 points higher report about 6 points more effort on average. The between-person interval is wider because its precision depends on the number of learners, 36, while the within-person slope draws on the daily deviations of all learners.

The difference between the between-person and the within-person slope is the contextual effect (Mundlak 1978). It measures the association of the person mean with the outcome beyond the association implied by the within-person slope. A positive contextual effect indicates that learners with higher mean efficacy invest more effort than their daily relation between efficacy and effort predicts, which is consistent with stable characteristics, such as motivation or prior achievement, that raise both mean efficacy and mean effort.

contextual(wb_fit)
#>   variable   within   between   contextual     S.E.           95% CI        p
#> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   efficacy   0.4164    0.6266       0.2102   0.1021   [0.003, 0.417]   0.0469
#> 
#> scope = pooled,  model = within_between,  estimator = ols,  subject = .all,  subgroup = .all

The between-person slope exceeds the within-person slope by 0.21 (95% CI 0.003 to 0.42, p = .047). The lower bound of the interval lies close to zero, and the evidence for a difference between the two slopes is weak.

Lagged variables

Many hypotheses about within-person processes concern effects that unfold over time, such as whether the efficacy of a learner on one day predicts the effort of that learner on the following day. A test of such a hypothesis requires a predictor measured before the outcome. Temporal precedence is also a necessary condition for a causal interpretation. Two variables measured at the same time can each be the cause of the other, whereas a variable measured earlier can only act on a later outcome. A lagged variable establishes this order by pairing each observation with the preceding observation of the same person. With lag = 1, the column efficacy_lag1 holds, in each row, the efficacy of the learner on the preceding day.

The pairing yields two kinds of lagged effect. The autoregressive effect, the slope of a variable on its own lagged value, measures the persistence of a state from one occasion to the next, often termed inertia. The cross-lagged effect, the slope of one variable on the lagged value of another, measures whether a deviation in one state precedes a deviation in the other, for example whether efficacy above a learner’s mean on one day predicts effort above the mean on the next day. These two effects are the parameters of the vector autoregressive models that underlie dynamic networks (Bringmann et al. 2013; Epskamp et al. 2018). Precedence is a necessary condition and remains insufficient on its own, since a third variable that changes before both can produce a cross-lagged association.

Lags are computed within persons, so each lagged value comes from the same person as the row it occupies. The first observation of each person has no preceding observation and receives a missing lagged value, as the first days of Aisha show.

lagged <- preprocess_panel(srl, id = "name", time = "day", vars = "efficacy", lag = 1, keep_all = FALSE)
head(lagged)
#>    name day efficacy efficacy_lag1
#> 1 Aisha   1 38.23529            NA
#> 2 Aisha   2 14.70588      38.23529
#> 3 Aisha   3 67.64706      14.70588
#> 4 Aisha   4 55.88235      67.64706
#> 5 Aisha   5 55.88235      55.88235
#> 6 Aisha   6 44.11765      55.88235

Of the 5,616 lagged values, 42 are missing, 36 for the first days of the learners and 6 for days that follow a day without an efficacy rating.

The size of a lagged effect depends on the interval between occasions. An effect that unfolds within hours appears stronger over a lag of one hour than over a lag of one day, and lagged effects are therefore comparable only between designs with similar intervals (Gollob and Reichardt 1987). A lag refers to the preceding occasion whatever the elapsed time, which is appropriate when occasions are evenly spaced, as the consecutive days in srl are for every learner. In designs with irregular spacing, such as experience sampling at random times or diaries with skipped days, lag_max_gap sets the lagged value to missing when the preceding occasion lies further back than a specified interval, so that a lag spanning several days stays out of a model of day-to-day effects.

Detrending

The within-person models of the later vignettes assume that each series is stationary, with a mean and a variance that stay constant over the study period. A series that rises or falls systematically violates this assumption. Its deviations from the person mean are then dominated by the trend, negative early in the study and positive late in the study, and an autoregressive model attributes the resulting dependence between neighbouring occasions to the persistence of the state. When two variables share a trend, their deviations correlate across occasions whatever their day-to-day relation, a spurious association well documented for time series (Granger and Newbold 1974). Detrending regresses the series of each person on time and retains the residuals, so that the within-person component expresses the fluctuation around the trajectory of the person (Wang and Maxwell 2015).

Removing a trend is a substantive decision. A trend can be a nuisance, such as a gradual habituation to the questionnaire, or the phenomenon of interest, such as a growth in efficacy over a course. In the second case detrending removes the effect under study, and time belongs in the model as a predictor.

preprocess_panel(detrend = "person") fits a linear trend to the series of each person and removes it when the slope is significant at detrend_alpha, 0.05 by default. The presence of trends is assessed beforehand with the trend tests that describe_persons() reports for each person and variable.

trends <- describe_persons(srl, id = "name", time = "day", vars = "efficacy:organizing", detail = "full")
summary(trends)
#>     variable persons mean_of_means sd_of_means mean_sd_within
#> 1    control      36      52.75783    18.45740       22.84994
#> 2   efficacy      36      54.03965    15.90734       21.27906
#> 3     effort      36      58.97604    14.54039       22.25366
#> 4       help      36      62.07208    18.17278       20.59724
#> 5 monitoring      36      49.11049    21.00157       21.10374
#> 6 organizing      36      55.49354    15.95229       22.35608
#> 7   planning      36      56.84187    14.86661       21.97606
#> 8     social      36      56.64708    21.02848       21.07529
#> 9      value      36      56.55765    14.53585       22.03823
#>   significant_trends trend_share
#> 1                  2  0.05555556
#> 2                  1  0.02777778
#> 3                  1  0.02777778
#> 4                  0  0.00000000
#> 5                  1  0.02777778
#> 6                  1  0.02777778
#> 7                  5  0.13888889
#> 8                  3  0.08333333
#> 9                  2  0.05555556

Across the nine variables, 16 of the 324 person-by-variable series (4.9%) have a significant linear trend. With 324 tests at the 0.05 level and no trend in any series, about 16 significant results are expected by chance. The observed count therefore gives no evidence of systematic trends, and detrending these data would alter a small number of series largely at random. Detrending is warranted when significant trends are considerably more frequent than the significance level, or when the design implies a trend, as in intervention or developmental studies.

A linear detrend suits a deterministic trend, a steady change in the mean. A stochastic trend, as in a random walk, wanders without a fixed slope and is removed by differencing, the replacement of each value by its change from the preceding occasion. preprocess(detrend = "auto") tests each series for both kinds of trend and applies linear detrending or differencing to the flagged series only.

Centring and scaling

Centring subtracts a mean from each score. The mean that is subtracted decides whether the differences between persons remain in the scores, and therefore whether a slope estimated on the centred scores is a within-person effect. Person-centring (center = "person") subtracts the person mean from each score and retains only the within-person component. It is the appropriate transformation when the research question concerns within-person processes alone, as in dynamic network models. In a multilevel autoregressive model, lagged predictors left uncentred carry the between-person differences in level, and the autoregressive effect then mixes the persistence of daily states with the stable differences between persons (Hamaker and Grasman 2015). Grand-mean centring (center = "grand") subtracts one mean computed over all persons and occasions. It gives the intercept the interpretation of the expected outcome at the sample mean and leaves the between-person differences in the scores, so a slope on grand-mean-centred scores remains the combination of the within-person and the between-person slope (Enders and Tofighi 2007). Person-centring and decomposition are alternatives, because person-centring discards the between-person component that decomposition retains, and preprocess_panel() refuses a request for both.

Scaling sets the unit of a variable. Person scaling (scale = "person") divides the scores of each person by that person’s standard deviation. Slopes then express change in standard deviations of the person, which makes them comparable across persons who fluctuate to different degrees. In srl, the within-person standard deviation of efficacy ranges from 14.7 to 34.5 points across learners. Person scaling also removes these differences in variability, and within-person variability is itself an individual difference with substantive meaning, such as emotional instability. A slope on person-scaled scores combines the strength of an association with the variability of the predictor and reports the two as one quantity. Grand scaling (scale = "grand") divides all scores by one standard deviation, which changes the unit of measurement and preserves the differences in variability between persons.

preprocess_panel() and split_levels() compute person means, standard deviations and trends from all occasions of each person. When a model is evaluated on held-out occasions, quantities computed from all occasions carry information from the held-out occasions into the estimation and inflate the measured predictive accuracy. fit_within_between() therefore computes the person means from the estimation occasions only and applies them to the held-out occasions, and the transformations of preprocess_panel() are suited to descriptive analyses and to models estimated without held-out occasions.
